prize_parts.citation: For the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enable in vivo delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are a self-assembly and colloid-chemistry solution to a problem that blocked nucleic-acid medicines for decades: how to carry a large, highly charged polyanion through the circulation and across an endosomal membrane. The design principle is crisp and general. A lipid whose charge is pKa-tuned is near-neutral at physiological pH, which keeps the particle inert in blood, and becomes cationic in the acidifying endosome, where it drives a change in lipid phase and membrane destabilization that releases the cargo. Rapid-mixing assembly and PEG-lipid control of particle size are further physical-chemical controls. This is chemistry about molecular organisation, not only a product, and its consequences are unusually well validated: patisiran and the mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. Maturity is not in question; the mechanism has been independently confirmed for over a decade. After the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside modification, the delivery chemistry that made that work usable is the missing half of the story, and it clearly belongs to Chemistry.
statement.case_against: The credit is the hardest problem. Six names are listed, Hope and Madden were early contributors in the Vancouver group, Langer is a major figure in delivery materials, and the three-person cap forces exclusions that a careful historian of ionizable-lipid priority could dispute. Part of the record is entangled with patent and commercial history that I cannot verify from the files. There is also a real risk that the committee reads this as a second prize for the mRNA-vaccine story. Finally, I am drawn to this as a lipid scientist, so I should be careful not to overweight it just because it is close to my own field.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks lipid nanoparticles first as a game-changer in which simple chemistry (pKa tuning, rapid-mixing assembly, PEG-lipids) had a decisive effect, and proposes Cullis, MacLachlan and Anderson with Hope, Madden and Langer excluded by the cap.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the trio, and I reached the same three names independently. I would qualify one thing: excluding Hope and Madden is a choice about which step counts as decisive, not a clean fact. I would defend Cullis as the anchor of the formulation concept and MacLachlan for the ionizable-lipid optimisation that made systemic siRNA work. Anderson's lipidoid libraries are a distinct route to ionizable lipids. If the committee prefers the Vancouver core, a Cullis, Madden, Hope trio is the principled alternative, as Chabes proposes, but it loses the later lipid-design step that connects to the clinical products.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks biomolecular phase separation last on his list because the in vivo evidence standard for condensates is still disputed, and he doubts it fits Chemistry rather than Physiology or Medicine.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge to my own opening first choice, and it moves me. I still think the concept (multivalent interactions, phase diagrams, wetting) is physical chemistry, but I cannot claim the interpretation is settled. Which cellular condensates are equilibrium phase separation, and which are overexpression artefacts, is exactly what a Nobel statement would have to be careful about. I therefore no longer rank it above a candidate with a validated mechanism and a clinical record, though I keep it as my first alternative and would revisit it in some years.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first as a general, mature method that changed how chemists build bonds, with Buchwald and Hartwig as the clean pair and Kosugi's tin-amide work as a precursor.
responses.response: I accept the maturity and the clean two-person attribution, and I take your point that C-N is not duplicative of the C-C chemistry honoured in 2010. My qualification is about relative novelty. Zou is right that it is a different bond type, but Chabes and Linke both see it as an extension of a field already recognised, and I give that some weight because lipid nanoparticles open a new class of medicine that did not exist as a modality. I am not arguing that C-N coupling is not worthy. It is a strong candidate and I keep it as my second alternative, since a majority of the committee may well see the case as cleaner than mine.

responses.point: Linke ranks the Car-Parrinello method first for its unambiguous two-name attribution and four decades of use, and ranks phase separation third as conceptually original but perhaps slightly early.
responses.response: I share your concern on phase separation and have shifted accordingly. On Car-Parrinello, I do not dispute the clean attribution or maturity. I wonder, as Aqvist does, whether the committee wants another purely theoretical or methods award after 2013 and 2024. I would like to hear how you weigh clean credit against a discovery with this kind of reach beyond chemistry itself.

uncertainties: Which three of Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer are most decisive, given patent and publication history I cannot verify.
Whether the committee will see ionizable lipid delivery as separable from the 2023 Medicine prize on mRNA.
Whether the evidence standard for condensates will have settled enough in a few years to make phase separation a stronger first choice.
How much weight the committee gives clean attribution and maturity (Pd C-N coupling, Car-Parrinello) against novelty of modality.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: I have no stated personal or institutional connection to any shortlisted candidate. I note that my research on lipid self-assembly is close to the lipid nanoparticle topic, which is a scientific closeness rather than a recusal issue, and that Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai are Lund colleagues on the committee but not candidates.
